newsitem.title: MEXICO: Internet, banks, deals top issues for insurers.
newsitem.headline: Internet, banks, deals top issues for insurers.

text.p: Global insurers face stiff challenges over the next few years as the Internet, banking deregulation, massive consolidation and risk securitization profoundly change the insurance landscape, speakers at a conference here this week said.
"We are seeing a number of changes which are going to be truly transformational," CNA Financial Corp chief executive Dennis Chookaszian said in his presentation at the conference on Monday.
Over 450 executives, academics and other insurance industry members from 47 countries attended the 33rd annual seminar sponsored by the International Insurance Society.
The four-day seminar featured 22 chief executives from 14 countries and they repeatedly stressed these main themes, some of which are already having an impact on the industry.

One is consolidation, which is already taking place in the global insurance industry at a rapid pace. But banking deregulation will take merger and acqusition activity to a whole new level, Gary Parr, head of Morgan Stanley's global insurance group told the conference on Wednesday.
"The change that is coming is going to be extraordinary," he said.

Indeed, Chubb Corp chief executive Dean O'Hare said he expects new competitors to include such financial service giants as General Electric Co's GE Capital, Citicorp, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover & Co, Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, Deutsche Bank and Union Bank of Switzerland in his presentation on Monday.
"The insurance industry of the year 2007 will look very, very different than it does today," O'Hare said.
"Many of the major players will be the same. But we will be contending with some powerful new competitors as well," he said.

"The deregulation and convergence of financial services is already well underway on a global scale and I believe it will accelerate as the last regulatory barriers in the U.S. are swept aside," he said.
And risk securitization, the transfer of insurance risk to the capital markets, will be among the services offered by new competitors like the investment banks.
CNA's Chookaszian told Reuters after his presentation on Monday that he believes risk securitization will develop into a robust market within 15 years.
Meanwhile, mutual companies, unable to raise capital the way publicly-traded stock companies can, will undergo major restructurings, Morgan Stanley's Parr said.
"We believe that will be a dramatic trend," Parr told the conference.
Insurers today also are grappling with how to use the Internet to distribute their products.
Chookaszian told the conference he believes electronic commerce will become an important part of the insurance business in the next five to 10 years.
"The Internet and Net-like communication is going to be a significant transformational idea on the industry," he said.
Global expansion also was a popular theme, with most insurers expressing interest in the growth potential of the Latin American or Asian markets.
Chubb's O'Hare said the Warren, N.J.-based company expects one-third of its premiums to come from outside of the United States by 2005.
Deregulation, economic growth and political stability are turning some of those previously-closed markets into more attractive places for foreigners to do business, the speakers said.
Gary Countryman, chief executive of Boston-based Liberty Mutual Insurance Co, discussed his company's success in using direct marketing techniques in the Mexican personal auto insurance market.
And several speakers mentioned Brazil as an important market in which to establish a presence.
"The global economy is not only hard to ignore, it's dangerous to ignore," O'Hare said.
